messages.subject: GeneActiv: wrong dates when battery has died
messages.subject_clean: GeneActiv: wrong dates when battery has died
messages.body_plain:
Hi all and happy new year!

Using GeneActiv in research, it sometimes happens that a participant brings the device back several months later than expected. After several hours of recharging, the data can still be extracted and are correct, except for one thing: the start time and config time in the *.bin file will be wrong (in my experience, always some date in 2010). In addition, the measurement frequency is always recorded as 100Hz.

As an example, a participant started wearing the device in 2023-09-16 21:00:00:000, but the relevant rows in the bin file look like this:

Measurement Frequency:100 Hz
...
Start Time:2010-09-16 09:10:00:000
...
Config Time:2010-09-16 09:08:54:000

However, the "recorded data" block has correct dates and looks like this:

Recorded Data
...
Sequence Number:0
Page Time:2023-09-16 21:00:00:500
...
Measurement Frequency:85.7
04FF6CF3B00004DF6FF3D00004DF6FF3B00004B.
...

So far, I have analyzed such files by manually changing the dates in the files (I've used the text editor called nano in linux terminal, but I suppose something like Notepad++ can be used in Windows -- the raw files are usually way too large for Notepad). The lines can also be changed programmatically (e.g., in R, using readLines and writeLines line by line). But it would be useful if GGIR would have the capability to detect such errors, issue a warning, and maybe use the first "Page time" instead of "Start time" in such cases. The only thing I do not understand is that the first "page time" seems to be 500 milliseconds later than the actual start time (the devices were set up to start recording at 21:00 sharp - to catch the sleep time before the first full day - but the "page time" is 21:00:00:500). For my purposes changing it to 500 ms earlier has solved the issue but I don't know why this happens, so I can't say this is the general solution.

Thank you and best regards,
Kenn Konstabel

When the battery runs out of charge, on being re-powered the date on the device returns to 2010 – this is designed behaviour as the device has no other reference. In certain circumstances, some of the header fields are also updated with test data – not a design feature, but it does not impact the recorded data."

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hello, I am using the Axivity AX6 accelerometers to carry out a study of physical activity in patients with cardiac pathology between 40 and 65 years of age.
When I run the code in RStudio using the last version of GGIR package (3.0.3), and with the default cut-points that appear in the code (30mg Light PA, >100mg MVPA), the average minutes of PA per day for each intensity are quite high, because, for example, the most patients exceed the weekly PA minutes recommended by the World Health Organization in just one day... However, the data for the MX metrics, intensity gradient or average acceleration, are consistent with values from other studies in similar populations.
I don't understand why these high values are reported for the PA minutes... I hope you can help me, I copy below the code used:

> library(GGIR)

> GGIR(mode=c(1,2,3,4,5),

+      datadir="entrada",

+      outputdir="salida",

+      do.report=c(2,4,5),

+      #=====================

+      # Part 2

+      #=====================

+      strategy = 1,

+      hrs.del.start = 0,          hrs.del.end = 0,

+      maxdur = 16,                 includedaycrit = 16,

+      qwindow=c(0,24),

+      mvpathreshold =c(100),

+      excludefirstlast = FALSE,

+      includenightcrit = 16,

+      qlevels = c(c(960/1440),c(1320/1440),c(1380/1440),c(1410/1440),c(1425/1440),c(1430/1440),c(1435/1440),c(1438/1440)),

+     iglevels = TRUE,

+      #=====================

+      # Part 3 + 4

+      #=====================

+      def.noc.sleep = 1,

+      outliers.only = TRUE,

+      criterror = 4,

+      do.visual = TRUE,

+      #=====================

+      # Part 5

+      #=====================

+      threshold.lig = c(30), threshold.mod = c(100),  threshold.vig = c(400),

+      boutcriter = 0.8,      boutcriter.in <http://boutcriter.in> = 0.9,     boutcriter.lig = 0.8,

+      boutcriter.mvpa = 0.8, boutdur.in <http://boutdur.in> = c(1,10,30), boutdur.lig = c(1,10),

+      boutdur.mvpa = c(1),

+      includedaycrit.part5 = 2/3,

+      #=====================

+      # Visual report

+      #=====================

+      timewindow = c("WW"),

+      visualreport=TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marcos

First off, two general questions: what was the wear location (wrist, hip, thigh)? and are you sure you made the right choice of using 100 mg as a cut-point for the axivity? As you know, cut-points are device, wear location, and population specific.

And a general comment: It is not advisable to compare cut-point-based accelerometer metrics to the WHO guidelines. Reason for that is that the WHO guidelines are currently predominantly questionnaire-based. Since accelerometers and questionnaires assess different constructs of PA with different granularity, comparison is faulty. A better way of approaching this is: a) if you want to stick to using cut-point-based metrics, compare the results to other studies using the same device and cut-points. Here would be one study in patients with heart failure using wrist-worn GENEActiv and a 100 mg threshold for MVPA (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34775952/).  Or b) consider using cut-point-free metrics and interpret your findings in relation to available reference values/ centile curves (i.e. AvAcc and IG) or use MXmetrics to translate your findings into sth meaningful. For option b), the following might be helpful: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37703330/

Cheers

Fabian

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Happy new year.

I have a query regarding some confusion over a physical activity data output. As part of the physical activity tracking, I am also reporting wear time in days (0-10) and valid weekday days and weekend days. So far (173 rows), 0 participants have a total of 10 days valid weekend and weekdays added up, even though there are lots of cases where wear time equals 9.8> (many cases of 9.99) across the 10 day collection period.  This seems a bit of odds with each other. I believe the missing day of data is originating from weekdays, but it could potentially be weekend days too. My thinking behind weekdays being the issue is that across any 10 day period we could feasibly see at one side of a continuum a maximum of 8 weekdays and 2 weekend days and at the other side of the continuum 6 weekdays and 4 weekend days. We see in our data instances of the maximum 4 weekend days, however we have no instances of the 8 day maximum weekday data (and checking the calendar of start dates, and cross referencing this with wear time data, we should see some instances of this).

For context
Accelerometers: ActiGraph and Axivity AX6 (this happens in both accelerometer type outputs)
Valid wear time is 16> hours across a day
We are analysing our data using R Studio and GGIR. We have gone over our script and there is nothing we can see that would limit the reporting of valid weekday or weekend day.
Question:
Why Am I not seeing some (where you would expect (e.g., 9.99 days wear time across a 10 day period) valid weekday and weekend days totalling 10?
What could be causing this loss of a days recording? (reminder, I think this is originating from weekdays)
Has anyone come across this issue before? If so, what was the solution you found, if there was one?
Many thanks for you help!

Gareth

> > > the performance of the non-wear detection for studies with different
> > > sensor attachment locations because we make all kinds of tiny
> > > movements with our body parts, which will trigger the wear-detection
> > > as soon as there is more variance in the data than would be expected
> > > from sensor noise. If you are in doubt then just do some experiments
> > > on yourself to see how GGIR handles an inactive day in the office or
> > > an evening behind the television and then investigate whether the code
> > > detects all your inactivity correctly as monitor-wear time.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > So, I can expect no misclassification between sedentary time and non-wear time due to these tiny movements that we produce even in hip (for example). Definitely I will prove it. I assume that using activity counts this misclassification is more likely because of all the smoothing process applied to the signal (they consider sedentary equal to non-wear time, =0 counts/min). I think this is one of the major advantages of working with raw data. Do you think that it is possible to apply smaller windows for non-wear detection (15 min instead of 60 min) without get a misclassification between these variables? I will prove on my own but I would like to know if you have already tested it.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > - The sleep detection algorithm is essentially a description of the
> > > data, as in: did the accelerometer orientation change by more than A
> > > degrees over a time window of B minutes. In my opinion there is
> > > nothing body location specific about that. Only when the
> > > wrist-specific parameters (5 degrees and 5 minutes) which I evaluated
> > > in last year’s paper are entered then the sleep detection will become
> > > wrist specific. So, in other words: A new set of parameters may make
> > > the algorithm equally well suitable for any other body location. All
> > > you need is a dataset to demonstrate that your new parameters are
> > > plausible for your new sensor location.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Totally agree, thank you for the explanation. Maybe in hip placement the sleeplogs should be compulsory to use since sedentary people can register similar angle patterns in their hips during wake time.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > 2- MVPA cut-points: I've seen that MVPA time detection is done through
> > > cut-points based on different metrics (most of them on ENMO). I think
> > > this method is similar to the one applied with counts, and then it can
> > > have the same limitations. What is your opinion about that? Do you
> > > trust in cut-point methods to detect MVPA or do you know other methods
> > > that have been tested?
> > >
> > > >>> Answer: I am aware of the limitations of cut-points. I do not think that there is a convincing alternative approach available. Cut-points are easy to replicate which is good for methodological consistency, and easy to evaluate and update even by non-technical users. The relationship between acceleration and human energy expenditure is complex. Within single activity types the relationship between acceleration and energy expenditure may seem fairly linear. However, the linear relationship has a different slope and y-intercept between activity types (see my 2009 publication in Obesity), and those differences between activity types are in turn also dependent on body weight and age of the person being measured. So, if we consider real life conditions with a variety of activity types and a variety of individuals then the relationship between acceleration and energy expenditure is highly non-linear. One of the key problems in dealing with this non-linearity is that a substantial part of the non-linearity is actually caused by the energy expenditure construct itself and not by the limitations of the accelerometer. For example, MET values for the activity type sitting differ hugely between lean and overweight individuals, while the entire PA research community assumes that MET values are constant per activity types across individuals of the same age. Especially, in the activity type sitting it is impossible to blame the accelerometer because the accelerometer shows zero movement across individuals. Therefore, I have always been surprised to see that there are people who try to estimate MET values in sedentary activity types. There is no form of machine learning that can address this problem because this is a matter of measurement construct and not a problem of classification. IN conclusion, I think it is best to stick with cut-points because they at least have some informative value: higher is more movement of the accelerometer. This may not always be directly related to energy expenditure of the person as a whole, which warrants careful interpretation of acceleration data as proxy for energy expenditure. My personal view would be to stop attempting to say anything about energy expenditure with accelerometer data and use acceleration itself as the ground truth for physical activity, e.g. cut-points thresholds informed by acceleration values across activity types rather than informed by acceleration values across energy expenditure levels.

> > >
> > > Very interesting reasoning. Regarding energy expenditure in sedentary activities, and in concordance with my question above on non-wear time, I agree with you in trying to estimate MET values through activity counts is an impossible task during strictly defined sedentary activities (no movement, no counts). But using raw accelerations, as you said before we always do tiny movements, then, wouldn't be easier to adress this question with raw data? Anyway, we would always have the variance inter-individuals as a major problem (even using biometric data in the models it would be very difficult to solve). However, I think that your opinion about using acceleration values themselves is the best option. We would need reference parameters in different populations to correctly understand the data, but I think that it is the best way to exploit the potential of accelerometers
> > >

> >
> > >

> > >
> > >
> > > > 4- Sleep time: Could you explain how to enter a sleeplog manually? It have to be done file with the arguments sleeplog_onset and sleeplog_wake? or is ther any easier method? > > >
> > > >>> Answer: See attached document as example
> >

> > >
> > >
> > > > Thanks again for your work!
> > > > Best regards,
> > > > Jairo Hidalgo Migueles

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brendan,

I think that what you see is expected and it is not related to GGIR. There are minor differences on how actilife stores de accelerations in the gt3x and the csv files, especially if the idle sleep mode was activated during the data collection. When using gt3x files, GGIR takes care of the time gap imputation, but in the csv files, the data are already imputed by the manufacturer and then minor differences are to be expected.

Best,
Jairo

messages.subject_clean: help needed = wear time overestimation in part 5 day & person summary - why/how to correct this?
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am analyzing data from actigraphs gt3x worn only during the day over 7 days with minimum of 10h/day, but I do not understand why do the part5_person and day reports overestimate wear time (dur_day_min) by a couple of hours in all 40 subjects that I have. Patients wore sensors 10-18h/day, but the part5 person summary gives dur-day-min  >1000minutes/day (>16h/day) for almost each day which is by inspection of individual file summaries not possible. How to correct this (if it needs to be corrected)?

Part5 reports divide 24h period (1440 minutes) into dur_day and dur_spt, but I do not understand how can the sum of dur_day and dur_spt can give the total of 24h if patients do not wear actigraphs all day. Any advice on how to solve this?

- is this overestimation maybe related to the prespecified qwindow=c(0,24) in my script? Should I write a different code as my patients take off the actigraph during the night?

Please see my code below with an example of data for one patient and thank you for the assistance:

library(GGIR)
install.packages("read.gt3x")
g.shell.GGIR(
  mode=c(1,2,3,4,5),
  datadir="C:/aaa",
  outputdir="C:/bbb",
  do.report=c(2,5), #if I want to report sleep, then number 4 needs to be added
  desiredtz="Europe/Brussels",

#part1
  idloc=6,
  dynrange=NULL,#default value for this is dynrange=null which provides 8 gravity,
  do.enmo = TRUE,#this is default setting
  acc.metric = "ENMO",

#part2
  strategy=2,
  includedaycrit=10,
  qwindow=c(0,24),
  do.imp=TRUE,
  mvpathreshold=c(69.1),
  excludefirstlast=FALSE,

#Part 3 and 4
  timethreshold=(5),#5 is default for both time and angle tresholds
  anglethreshold=5,
  ignorenonwear=TRUE,#true is default for ignorenonwear
  def.noc.sleep=1, #1 is default for defnocsleep

#Part5
  threshold.lig=c(47.4),
  threshold.mod=c(69.1),
  threshold.vig=c(258.7) ,
  bout.criter=0.8,
  boutcriter.in <http://boutcriter.in>=0.9,
  boutcriter.lig=0.8,
  boutcriter.mvpa=0.8,
  boutdur.in <http://boutdur.in>=c(1, 10, 30),
  boutdur.lig=c(1, 10),
  boutdur.mvpa=c(1, 10),
  includedaycrit.part5=10,#includedaycrit would be 16hours if I had night measurement
  part5_agg2_60seconds = TRUE,

#visual report
  timewindow=c("MM"),
  visualreport=TRUE,
  week_weekend_aggregate.part5=TRUE)

> A couple more points to check if I understood correctly:

The sleep analysis are documented here:
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/GGIR.html#56_Sleep_analysis

There is no "sleep window", but there is a guider window, a sleep period time window, and under some conditions a Time in bed window. It is important that you understand the difference. For example, HorAngle or the sleep log defines the guider window. Their overlap with sustained inactivity bouts then defines when the estimated SPT window starts and ends. In the case of HorAngle or with some sleeplogs, sleepwindowType is set to TimeInBed which means that the window defined as HorAngle or reported in sleeplog is treated as time in bed and not self-reported SPT. When sleepwindowType is set to TimeInbed GGIR SPT is estimated differently sib that starts before or after time in bed is ignored from SPT.

We discuss this in more detail in our training: https://www.accelting.com/ggir-training/
Alternatively, you will have to wait till we have finished those chapters. I do not think there is much you can do now to help with that.

Best,
Vincent

> > > > <jairo.hidal...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > 1- About device placement: I believe that all algorithms (e.g. autocalibration, non-wear time and sleep time detection,...) implemented in GGIR have been developed for non-dominant wrist data, haven't it? If so, Could I expect a well-functioning of autocalibration (implemented with g.calibrate) for hip data? I think that non-wear detection and sleep algorithms are specific for device placement and they are not supposed to work well in hip for instance, have they been proved with hip data?
> > > >
> > > > >>> Answer: None the calculations in GGIR is body location specific and I have tried to design GGIR in a way that it could work for any body location. You a correct though that most of the work to support GGIR is based on wrist data, by which it is possible that GGIR is better justified for wrist data than for other body locations. However, I have good hope for its generic use for the following reasons:
> > > > - The auto-calibration algorithm relies on having sufficient
> > > > calibration points around the sphere (as explained in the 2014
> > > > paper). This may easier with wrist data than with hip data, but the
> > > > good thing about function g.calibrate is that it also evaluates its
> > > > own performance and will tell you whether the autocalibration was
> > > > successful; see QC output in GGIR. My experience is that the algorithm
> > > > works fine for hip data, but as I said you will always be able to
> > > > verify this yourself if in doubt.
> > > >
> > > > I am not sure to be agree in here. If I have understood well your 2014 paper, auto-calibration algorithm uses the time with no supposed body movement in which the acceleration measured should be only the gravitational one (=1g). And it is provided a correction factor based on that assumption (I understand that auto-calibration algorithm can work in any body location since it works with no-movement time, independently the placement). Then, considering that hip placement experiments more time without movement than wrist in free-living conditions, shouldn't get more data to populate the sphere using hip data?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > - Non-wear detection is by its own definition not body location
> > > > specific. The algorithm is based on the signal noise level over large
> > > > time windows, by default 1 hour. Therefore, I see no reason to doubt
> > > > the performance of the non-wear detection for studies with different
> > > > sensor attachment locations because we make all kinds of tiny
> > > > movements with our body parts, which will trigger the wear-detection
> > > > as soon as there is more variance in the data than would be expected
> > > > from sensor noise. If you are in doubt then just do some experiments
> > > > on yourself to see how GGIR handles an inactive day in the office or
> > > > an evening behind the television and then investigate whether the code
> > > > detects all your inactivity correctly as monitor-wear time.
> > > >
> > > > So, I can expect no misclassification between sedentary time and non-wear time due to these tiny movements that we produce even in hip (for example). Definitely I will prove it. I assume that using activity counts this misclassification is more likely because of all the smoothing process applied to the signal (they consider sedentary equal to non-wear time, =0 counts/min). I think this is one of the major advantages of working with raw data. Do you think that it is possible to apply smaller windows for non-wear detection (15 min instead of 60 min) without get a misclassification between these variables? I will prove on my own but I would like to know if you have already tested it.
> > > >
> > > > - The sleep detection algorithm is essentially a description of the
> > > > data, as in: did the accelerometer orientation change by more than A
> > > > degrees over a time window of B minutes. In my opinion there is
> > > > nothing body location specific about that. Only when the
> > > > wrist-specific parameters (5 degrees and 5 minutes) which I evaluated
> > > > in last year’s paper are entered then the sleep detection will become
> > > > wrist specific. So, in other words: A new set of parameters may make
> > > > the algorithm equally well suitable for any other body location. All
> > > > you need is a dataset to demonstrate that your new parameters are
> > > > plausible for your new sensor location.
> > > >

> > > > 2- MVPA cut-points: I've seen that MVPA time detection is done through
> > > > cut-points based on different metrics (most of them on ENMO). I think
> > > > this method is similar to the one applied with counts, and then it can

> > > > trust in cut-point methods to detect MVPA or do you know other methods
> > > > that have been tested?

> > > > >>> Answer: I am aware of the limitations of cut-points. I do not think that there is a convincing alternative approach available. Cut-points are easy to replicate which is good for methodological consistency, and easy to evaluate and update even by non-technical users. The relationship between acceleration and human energy expenditure is complex. Within single activity types the relationship between acceleration and energy expenditure may seem fairly linear. However, the linear relationship has a different slope and y-intercept between activity types (see my 2009 publication in Obesity), and those differences between activity types are in turn also dependent on body weight and age of the person being measured. So, if we consider real life conditions with a variety of activity types and a variety of individuals then the relationship between acceleration and energy expenditure is highly non-linear. One of the key problems in dealing with this non-linearity is that a substantial part of the non-linearity is actually caused by the energy expenditure construct itself and not by the limitations of the accelerometer. For example, MET values for the activity type sitting differ hugely between lean and overweight individuals, while the entire PA research community assumes that MET values are constant per activity types across individuals of the same age. Especially, in the activity type sitting it is impossible to blame the accelerometer because the accelerometer shows zero movement across individuals. Therefore, I have always been surprised to see that there are people who try to estimate MET values in sedentary activity types. There is no form of machine learning that can address this problem because this is a matter of measurement construct and not a problem of classification. IN conclusion, I think it is best to stick with cut-points because they at least have some informative value: higher is more movement of the accelerometer. This may not always be directly related to energy expenditure of the person as a whole, which warrants careful interpretation of acceleration data as proxy for energy expenditure. My personal view would be to stop attempting to say anything about energy expenditure with accelerometer data and use acceleration itself as the ground truth for physical activity, e.g. cut-points thresholds informed by acceleration values across activity types rather than informed by acceleration values across energy expenditure levels.

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] help needed = wear time overestimation in part 5 day & person summary - why/how to correct this?
messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] help needed = wear time overestimation in part 5 day & person summary - why/how to correct this?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Tin,

Variable dur_day_min is not the duration the sensor is worn, but the duration of the waking hours in a window.

Note that argument includedaycrit.part5 is specific to the waking hours of the day (I will have to improve documentation for that). In part 5 we do not look at number of valid hours in the full window, we only consider number of valid hours during waking hours or ratio of valid hours during the waking hours of the day. Non-wear during the night is intentionally not accounted for because the focus of part 5 is time-use and not sleep research. This is why most of your days meet the inclusion criteria. So, if you specify 10 hours, it will check that the waking hours have a proportion of at least 10/24 (41.7%) valid hours. I would advise change that back to the default as this seems too low.

> Part5 reports divide 24h period (1440 minutes) into dur_day and dur_spt, but I do not understand how can the sum of dur_day and dur_spt can give the total of 24h if patients do not wear actigraphs all day. Any advice on how to solve this?

Time is recording time irrespective of wear or not wear. Therefore, we always expect these to add up to 24 hours if the window definition is MM (midnight-midnight). The aim in part 5 is to characterise time-use, which requires that every minute of the day is accounted for and missing data is imputed. Given that we do not want to rely on imputation too heavily it is best to exclude days with a lot of non-wear during waking hours, which is why includedaycrit.part5 is 2/3 by default.

Best, Vincent

Dr. Vincent van Hees | Independent consultant | https://accelting.com/

Hi Lara,

I think your expectation is not correct. GGIR estimates sleep by combining sleeplog (guider) and acc-based sustained inactivity bouts (sibs): The sibs that overlap with the guider define the exact sleep onset and wakeup time. The vignette also makes an attempt to explain that. This is why sleep onset and wakeup time are unlikely to match exactly the sleeplog.

If you do not trust the accelerometer and want to fully rely on the guider (your sleeplog) then set argument relyonguider = TRUE, however I intentionally did not use that as default because often we want to rely on the accelerometer to tell us the exact timing while the sleeplog is nothing more than a way to help guide the accelerometer, hence the name guider.

Best wishes,

Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Dear all

I wanted to use my R script of last year to process some extra Axivity files (.cwa), however the script I used last year doesn't seem to run anymore as I encounter an error in part 1... Below you can find the relevant code snippet:

folder_data = "C:/Users/vvoeckel/Documents/Verwerking Axivity data/"
folder_raw = paste0(folder_data, "1_raw/")
folder_ggi = paste0(folder_data, "1_gpart_meta/")

GGIR::g.part1(folder_raw, folder_ggi, f1 = length(dir(folder_raw)),
chunksize = 1, windowsizes = c(1, 900, 3600),
overwrite = FALSE, desiredtz = 'Europe/Brussels')

This is the error I get:

Error in gzfile(file, "wb") : cannot open the connection
In addition: Warning message:
In gzfile(file, "wb") :
cannot open compressed file 'C:/Users/vvoeckel/Documents/Verwerking Axivity data/1_gpart_meta//meta/basic/meta_621_PRE.cwa.RData', probable reason 'No such file or directory'

I have attempted to troubleshoot the issue by checking package updates, checking the directory existence, verifying permissions, using full file paths in the code (with and without "/" at the end), and testing the code on several files. Unfortunately, the problem persists.

Any insights or suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you in advance for your assistance!

Kind regards
Veerle Van Oeckel
